        <!-- Expandable Folded Methods & Assumptions -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('chirps_seasonal')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">
            <div class="decision-box">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                <span class="rationale-tag">Spatial Continuity Rationale</span>
              </div>
              <p class="rationale-text">
                <strong>The "Best Available Data" Reality:</strong> Ground-based meteorological stations in northern Kenya are extremely sparse—often fewer than one active, reliable rain gauge per 20,000 km². Relying purely on physical weather stations creates massive blind spots across ASAL pastoral rangelands. CHIRPS v3 (UCSB/CHC) blends cold-cloud duration satellite infrared with reporting stations to create continuous 5 km grids spanning 1981 to present. Satellite-gauge blending is the physically grounded standard to track pixel-level subcounty drought and flood anomalies continuously across Kenya.
              </p>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid">
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>WMO Climatological Baseline:</strong> Anomalies are computed against the 1991–2020 normal period (30 years) to conform to WMO standard reference rules.</li>
                  <li><strong>Linear Detrending:</strong> Long-term greenhouse gas warming trends are detrended before calculating ENSO/IOD teleconnection correlations to isolate interannual ocean forcing.</li>
                  <li><strong>Fixed Accumulation Windows:</strong> OND (Oct 1 – Dec 31) and MAM (Mar 1 – May 31) are treated as rigid seasonal boundaries matching agricultural calendars.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Limitations</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Orographic Underestimation:</strong> Thermal infrared satellite estimates systematically underestimate localized orographic rainfall around isolated mountain massifs (e.g. Mt. Marsabit, Mt. Kulal).</li>
                  <li><strong>SPEI Evapotranspiration:</strong> SPEI-3 utilizes Hargreaves-Samani PET, which can over-estimate evaporative demand during hyper-thermal arid spells.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="fold-footer-bar">
              <div><strong>Primary Source:</strong> CHIRPS v3 (0.05°) &bull; Vicente-Serrano SPEI-3 &bull; <code>s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=precipitation/source=chirps-v3/</code></div>
              <div class="fold-footer-actions">
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('chirps_seasonal')">CHIRPS Spec &rarr;</button>
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('spei_seasonal')">SPEI-3 Spec &rarr;</button>
              </div>
            </div>
          </div>
        </details>
      </div>

      <!-- Section 3.2: Empirical Contingency Matrix -->
      <div class="enso-figure-card" id="section-tercile-contingency" style="margin-top: 1.5rem;">
        <div class="enso-figure-header">
          <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
            <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
              <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 3.2</span>
              <h3 class="enso-figure-title">Empirical Contingency Probability Matrix (Tercile Likelihood given Ocean Driver Strength)</h3>
            </div>
            <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Observed conditional probabilities of Wetter, Near-normal, or Drier seasons conditioned on ENSO, IOD, and Western-V intensity classes (1981–2024 record).</p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Plain-Language How to Read -->
        <div class="enso-insight info" style="margin-bottom: 0.85rem; font-size: 0.84rem;">
          <strong>How to Read Tercile Probabilities:</strong> Historical seasons are stratified into equal thirds based on 1991–2020 climatology: <em>Wetter</em> (top 33.3%), <em>Near-normal</em> (middle 33.3%), and <em>Drier</em> (bottom 33.3%). Under random chance or neutral ocean conditions, each tercile has an unconditional base rate of ~33%. Shifts away from 33% quantify the empirical teleconnection strength.
        </div>

        <!-- Toolbar Host for Figure 3.2 Controls -->
        <div id="sec22ControlsHost" class="enso-control-bar"></div>

        <!-- Host Div for Figure 3.2 Plot -->
        <div id="plotContingencyHost" style="min-height: 360px; width: 100%;"></div>

        <!-- Teleconnection Insight Box -->
        <div id="sec22InsightHost" style="margin-top: 0.75rem;"></div>

        <!-- Figure 3.2 plotFooter Host -->
        <div id="fig32FooterHost"></div>

        <!-- Expandable Folded Methods & Assumptions -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('teleconnections')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">
            <div class="decision-box">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                <span class="rationale-tag">Non-Parametric Teleconnection Evidence</span>
              </div>
              <p class="rationale-text">
                <strong>Honest Physical Limits:</strong> Standard linear correlation models oversimplify East African climate teleconnections because rainfall responses are asymmetric and non-linear. The empirical contingency matrix stratifies the historical 44-year record into discrete ocean driver intensity bands (Strong, Moderate, Neutral/Weak) and computes the exact empirical tercile distribution (Wetter / Near-normal / Drier) for each state. This gives planners non-parametric, physically transparent probabilities directly matching KMD 3-tier seasonal forecasts.
              </p>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid">
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Tercile Climatological Equal-Likelihood:</strong> Under climatology, each tercile (Wet, Near, Dry) has an unconditional base rate of 33.3% over the 1991–2020 normal period.</li>
                  <li><strong>Small-Sample Transparency:</strong> Groups with fewer than 4 historical seasons are explicitly flagged with an asterisk (*) to warn against interpreting isolated anecdotes as statistical proof.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Limitations</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Sample Size Constraints:</strong> Super El Niño and Super +IOD events are rare extremes (n = 3–5 events in 44 years), limiting sample sizes for extreme composite bins.</li>
                  <li><strong>MAM Driver Independence:</strong> The Western-V gradient partially decouples from equatorial Pacific ENSO during the Long Rains (MAM), reflecting subtropical Western North Pacific wave trains.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="fold-footer-bar">
              <div><strong>Primary Source:</strong> NOAA CPC ONI &bull; HadISST / ERSST DMI &bull; CHIRPS v3 Terciles &bull; <code>s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=indices/</code></div>
              <div class="fold-footer-actions">
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('teleconnections')">Teleconnection Spec &rarr;</button>
              </div>
            </div>
          </div>
        </details>
      </div>

      <!-- Section 3.3: Oceanic Driver Teleconnection Relationships -->
      <div class="enso-figure-card" id="section-driver-scatter" style="margin-top: 1.5rem;">
        <div class="enso-figure-header">
          <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
            <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
              <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 3.3</span>
              <h3 class="enso-figure-title">How Strongly Do Equatorial Ocean Temperatures Govern County Rainfall?</h3>
            </div>
            <p class="enso-figure-purpose">Candidate ocean driver comparison table, continuous bivariate scatter distribution, and linear regression across all 44 historical seasons (1981–2024).</p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Candidate Driver Comparison Table Host -->
        <div id="sec23DriverTableHost" style="margin-bottom: 1rem;"></div>

        <!-- Toolbar Host for Figure 3.3 Controls -->
        <div id="sec23ScatterControlsHost" class="enso-control-bar"></div>

        <!-- Stats Callout Host for Figure 3.3 -->
        <div id="sec23ScatterStatsHost" style="margin-top: 0.5rem;"></div>

        <!-- Host Div for Figure 3.3 Reactive Plot -->
        <div id="plotDriverScatterHost" style="min-height: 380px; width: 100%; margin-top: 0.5rem;"></div>

        <!-- Figure 3.3 plotFooter Host -->
        <div id="fig33FooterHost"></div>

        <!-- Expandable Folded Methods & Assumptions -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('teleconnections')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">
            <div class="decision-box">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Why this data &amp; analysis?</span>
                <span class="rationale-tag">Continuous Teleconnection Sensitivity</span>
              </div>
              <p class="rationale-text">
                <strong>Bridging Discrete Bins to Continuous Sensitivity:</strong> While contingency matrices (Figure 3.2) group ocean drivers into coarse categorical bins, climate finance proposal writers and disaster contingency planners require exact marginal response metrics: for every +0.5°C or +1.0°C rise in equatorial Pacific SST (RONI) or Western Indian Ocean SST (DMI), how many additional millimetres or percentage points of rainfall are expected? This continuous scatter plot and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression line across all 44 historical years (1981–2024) provides the empirical slope, Pearson correlation coefficient (r), coefficient of determination (R²), and two-tailed p-value.
              </p>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid">
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Key Assumptions</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Climatological Normal:</strong> Anomalies are computed against the WMO standard 1991–2020 reference period.</li>
                  <li><strong>Linear Bivariate Modeling:</strong> OLS regression provides the linear teleconnection slope. Non-linear saturation effects during super-events (e.g. 1997, 2023) are visible as residual scatters from the trendline.</li>
                  <li><strong>Seasonal Alignment:</strong> OND rainfall is paired with OND ocean indices; MAM rainfall is paired with MAM ocean indices (Western-V / WNP).</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Caveats &amp; Statistical Power</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Collinearity:</strong> ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole often co-occur during OND (e.g. positive IOD + El Niño in 1997, 2006, 2019, 2023). Raw bivariate r reflects combined ocean basin influence; check the candidate table for multi-driver variance.</li>
                  <li><strong>Outlier Leverage:</strong> Extreme years like 1997 and 2023 exert leverage on the slope; points are explicitly labeled to inspect leverage.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

            <div class="fold-footer-bar">
              <div><strong>Primary Sources:</strong> NOAA CPC ONI &bull; HadISST DMI &bull; CHIRPS v3 &bull; <code>data/KE-enso-explorer/chirps_county.parquet</code></div>
              <div class="fold-footer-actions">
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('teleconnections')">Teleconnection Spec &rarr;</button>
                <button class="btn-dataset-jump" onclick="jumpToDataset('chirps_seasonal')">CHIRPS Spec &rarr;</button>
              </div>
            </div>
          </div>
        </details>
      </div>
</section>

<section id="tab-maps" class="tab-pane" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="btn-tab-maps">
      
      <!-- Section 3: Historical Climate Evidence (Part 3.2: Climate Maps) -->
      <div class="enso-section-header" style="margin-bottom: 1.25rem;">
        <div class="enso-section-eyebrow">3 Historical Climate Evidence &bull; 3.2 Climate Maps</div>
        <h2 class="enso-section-title">
          Section 3.2 &bull; Gridded Satellite Climate History &amp; Flood Diagnostics — <span class="county-name-txt">Marsabit</span>
        </h2>
        <p class="enso-section-lead">
          High-resolution pixel-by-pixel spatial raster maps across historical seasons and hydrodynamic flood exposure benchmarks.
        </p>
      </div>

      <!-- Section 3.4: Multi-Decadal Gridded Field History & Spatial Patterns -->
      <div class="enso-figure-card" id="section-raster-grid">
        <div class="enso-figure-header">
          <div class="enso-figure-header-main">
            <div class="enso-figure-title-row">
              <span class="enso-figure-number">Figure 3.4</span>
              <h3 class="enso-figure-title">Multi-Decadal Gridded Field History &amp; Spatial Patterns (Per-Year Field Canvas Grid)</h3>
            </div>
            <p class="enso-figure-purpose">High-resolution pixel-by-pixel spatial raster maps (CHIRPS v3, SPEI-3, MODIS NDVI, Copernicus GFM Flood, FEWS WRSI) across historical years, tinted by ocean teleconnection state.</p>
          </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Upfront Editorial Context: Why this data and analysis? -->
        <div class="enso-insight info" style="margin-bottom: 0.85rem;">
          <strong style="color: #0369a1;">Why Pixel-by-Pixel Verification Matters:</strong> County-level spatial averages mask extreme local gradients across Kenya's complex topography. By inspecting per-year gridded rasters across independent earth observation systems (CHIRPS v3 rainfall, SPEI-3 drought index, MODIS NDVI vegetation health, Copernicus GFM SAR satellite flood extent, and FEWS/USGS WRSI crop-water satisfaction), proposal teams and disaster managers can verify whether a regional teleconnection anomaly (e.g. 1997 or 2023 El Niño) penetrated into specific pastoral subcounties, grazing corridors, or highland agricultural zones.
        </div>

        <!-- Toolbar Host for Figure 3.4 Controls -->
        <div id="sec24ControlsHost" class="enso-control-bar"></div>

        <!-- Correlation Header & Teleconnection Guide Host -->
        <div id="sec24CorrHost" style="margin-top: 0.5rem;"></div>

        <!-- Dual Legend Host (Card Phase Tint + Raster Color Ramp + White Pixel) -->
        <div id="sec24LegendHost" style="margin: 0.5rem 0 0.85rem;"></div>

        <!-- Host Div for Figure 3.4 Interactive Grid / Loading UI -->
        <div id="plotRasterGridHost" style="min-height: 420px; width: 100%;"></div>

        <!-- Figure 3.4 plotFooter Host -->
        <div id="fig34FooterHost"></div>

        <!-- Standardized Modular Documentation Fold (4 Modules) -->
        <details class="enso-more-details">
          <summary>
            <span>Find out more (data, methods, limitations, and more)</span>
            <button type="button" class="enso-source-method-button" onclick="event.stopPropagation(); openMethodDrawer('chirps_seasonal')">Sources &amp; methods &rarr;</button>
          </summary>
          <div class="methods-fold-content">

            <!-- Module A: Visual Interpretation & Capabilities -->
            <div class="doc-module-card">
              <div class="rationale-heading">
                <span class="rationale-pill why-pill">Module A: Plot Capabilities &amp; Visual Interpretation</span>
              </div>
              <ul class="rationale-list" style="margin-top: 0.35rem;">
                <li><strong>Per-Year Facet Canvas:</strong> Renders 40+ years of high-resolution gridded satellite observations in an interactive multi-column grid, clipped to official IEBC county boundaries.</li>
                <li><strong>Ocean Teleconnection Tint:</strong> Each year card is subtly tinted by the standardized anomaly (<em>z</em>-score) of the selected oceanic driver (PRGn diverging palette by default: green for wet teleconnection states, purple for suppressing dry states).</li>
                <li><strong>Anomaly vs. Climatology:</strong> Rainfall displays standardized departure from the WMO 1991–2020 reference normal by default (&plusmn;300 mm scale), isolating true teleconnection impacts from baseline aridity.</li>
                <li><strong>Multi-Sensor Diagnostics:</strong> Switch between 5 earth observation systems to evaluate whether atmospheric moisture translated into surface drought (SPEI-3), vegetation biomass (NDVI), inundation (GFM), or crop satisfaction (WRSI).</li>
              </ul>
            </div>

            <div class="rationale-grid" style="margin-top: 0.75rem;">
              <!-- Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats -->
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Module B: Assumptions, Limitations &amp; Caveats</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Reference Climatology Baseline:</strong> Rainfall anomalies are computed against 1991–2020 WMO standard normal. SPEI-3 is already standard-normalized; MODIS NDVI and Copernicus GFM do not have 30-year baselines.</li>
                  <li><strong>Copernicus GFM Record Length &amp; SAR Masking:</strong> Sentinel-1 SAR flood coverage spans only 2018–2025. It reflects recent flood-proneness and orbital pass timing, NOT long-term return-period magnitude. Value 255 (unobserved swath) is strictly excluded as NoData, never counted as dry.</li>
                  <li><strong>HTTP Range COG Streaming:</strong> GeoTIFF rasters are window-read on the fly via HTTP range requests against AWS S3 CloudFront, fetching only the county bounding box to preserve client memory.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>

              <!-- Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary -->
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Module C: Methods &amp; Analysis Summary</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Driver Independence (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell):</strong> Correlation chips display bivariate Pearson <em>r</em> alongside partial correlation (controlling for other drivers) to eliminate double-counting of collinear ENSO and IOD signals.</li>
                  <li><strong>Multi-Driver Linear Combination:</strong> Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression calculates the optimal multi-driver variance explained (adjusted <em>R</em>&sup2;), identifying whether joint monitoring beats single indices.</li>
                  <li><strong>Phase Intensity Gating:</strong> Categorical intensity presets filter analogue historical seasons at |<em>z</em>| &ge; 1.0&sigma; (moderate) and |<em>z</em>| &ge; 1.5&sigma; (strong/extreme) thresholds.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

The European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC) GloFAS-Hazard v4.0 dataset provides 90 m hydrodynamic modeling derived from 2D LISFLOOD channel simulations (1979–2022). Toggling between observed footprints (2018–2025) and modelled probabilistic benchmarks gives planners a complete picture of contingent vulnerability.

              </div>
              <ul class="rationale-list" style="margin-top: 0.35rem;">
                <li><strong>Dual-Source Diagnostics:</strong> Toggle between observed satellite radar footprints (Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR) and modelled probabilistic benchmarks (EC JRC GloFAS 10- to 500-year return periods).</li>
                <li><strong>Multi-Scenario Comparison:</strong> Select multiple return period checkboxes (10 to 500 years) to compare the non-linear expansion of inundated territory against built infrastructure.</li>
                <li><strong>Population Denominators:</strong> Headcounts reflect official KNBS 2019 National Census totals distributed across WorldPop 100 m residential building footprints.</li>

              <!-- Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats -->
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill caveat-pill">Module B: Assumptions, Limitations &amp; Caveats</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>HOT-OSM Volunteer Gaps:</strong> Health center and school locations originate from crowdsourced Humanitarian OpenStreetMap (HOT-OSM). In remote pastoral counties, crowdsourced coverage is incomplete. <strong>A value of zero exposed schools reflects absence of volunteer mapped points, NOT immunity to floods.</strong></li>
                  <li><strong>Riverine vs. Flash Floods:</strong> GloFAS models riverine overtopping along major channel networks (Tana, Ewaso Ng'iro, Daua). It does not capture sudden convective cloudbursts flushing through dry sand-rivers (<em>laggas / wadis</em>).</li>
                  <li><strong>Stationarity Assumption:</strong> Return periods assume stationary hydrologic extremes over the 1979–2022 reanalysis window; intensifying warming may shift 100-year events into 50-year frequencies.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>

              <!-- Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary -->
              <div class="rationale-col">
                <div class="rationale-heading">
                  <span class="rationale-pill assumption-pill">Module C: Methods &amp; Analysis Summary</span>
                </div>
                <ul class="rationale-list">
                  <li><strong>Hydrodynamic Routing:</strong> 2D LISFLOOD hydrological model forced by GloFAS runoff, routing peak discharge through digital elevation models to compute water depth rasters.</li>
                  <li><strong>Spatial Exposure Intersect:</strong> Performed via DuckDB spatial polygon-in-raster operations, clipping depth surfaces at &ge; 0.15 m threshold across subcounty boundaries.</li>
                  <li><strong>Seasonal Asymmetry:</strong> OND floods are basin-wide riverine surges driven by El Niño and +IOD; MAM floods are localized flash floods driven by Western-V convective cloudbursts.</li>
                </ul>
              </div>
            </div>

          <div style="background: #f0fdf4; border: 1px solid #bbf7d0; border-left: 4px solid #16a34a; border-radius: 6px; padding: 0.85rem 1.15rem; margin-bottom: 1rem; font-size: 0.84rem; color: #166534; line-height: 1.5;">
            <strong>Terms of Trade (ToT) Economic Formulation &amp; Temporal Framing:</strong> Quantifies pastoral purchasing power as the kilograms of white maize grain purchased by selling one medium live goat:
            <div style="margin: 0.4rem 0; font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.95rem; font-weight: 700; color: #14532d;">
              ToT (kg maize / goat) = Retail Goat Price (KES / head) &divide; Retail Maize Grain Price (KES / kg)
            </div>
            In normal years across Marsabit, 1 goat purchases 65–75 kg of maize grain. During severe droughts, grazing collapses force distress livestock dumping (depressing goat prices), while grain prices soar. When ToT falls below the <strong>25 kg/goat emergency threshold</strong>, pastoral households experience catastrophic purchasing power collapse.<br>
            <strong>Methodological Framing Note:</strong> The severe &gt;50% purchasing power collapse holds strictly on <em>monthly purchasing power evaluated against trailing 24-month peaks</em> (August 2011: &minus;68.1% to 28.7 kg/goat; October 2022: &minus;65.4% to 33.4 kg/goat; February 2023: &minus;68.1% to 25.1 kg/goat across the full 2020&ndash;23 multi-season failure). Annual mean aggregation dampens these crisis troughs (2011: &minus;32.5%; 2022: &minus;37.6%) and masks acute seasonal distress. In addition, 2020 carries only 9 paired months in the sentinel series.
          </div>

The FEWS NET Data Warehouse (USAID) provides monthly retail and wholesale price monitoring across sentinel markets in 42 counties (2000–2026). This connects oceanic temperature anomalies directly to pastoral household purchasing power and acute hunger.

                    <li><strong>Terms-of-Trade (ToT) Ratio &mdash; derived, not sourced:</strong> Quantifies the purchasing power of pastoralists as the kilograms of maize grain purchased by the sale of one medium live goat. We compute it here as goat price &divide; maize price from the FEWS NET series; no agency publishes it. Being a ratio, a fall can mean <em>either</em> cheaper livestock <em>or</em> dearer grain &mdash; opposite implications for a herder &mdash; so read it alongside the two price legs above, never alone.</li>
                  </ul>

In accordance with CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO, IPC data are presented strictly for non-commercial reference and cited verbatim; they are never blended or merged into CC-BY-4.0 derived analytical layers.</li>

```{=html}
<section id="tab-science" class="tab-pane" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="btn-tab-science">
      
      <div class="science-paper">
        <header class="science-paper-header">
          <div class="science-eyebrow">Physical Teleconnections &amp; Analytical Foundations</div>
          <h2 class="science-main-title">How Equatorial Ocean Dynamics Govern Kenya's Rainfall and Agricultural Vulnerability</h2>
          <p class="science-abstract">
            An empirical and physical analysis of planetary atmospheric wave dynamics, ocean heat transport, and regional microclimates governing the October–December (Short Rains) and March–May (Long Rains) seasons across Kenya's 47 counties.
          </p>
          
          <!-- Audience Perspective Switcher -->
          <div class="view-switch-container">
            <span class="view-switch-label">Analytical view:</span>
            <div class="view-switch-group">
              <button class="view-switch-btn active" id="btn-track-lay" onclick="switchScienceTrack('lay')">
                Policy &amp; Planning Perspective
              </button>
              <button class="view-switch-btn" id="btn-track-tech" onclick="switchScienceTrack('tech')">
                Physical Dynamics &amp; Governing Equations
              </button>
            </div>
          </div>
        </header>

        <!-- SECTION 1: PACIFIC TO KENYA TELECONNECTION -->
        <article class="science-section">
          <div class="science-section-num">Section 01 &bull; Atmospheric Teleconnections</div>
          <h3 class="science-section-title">Theoretical Framework 5.1 &bull; Physical Teleconnection Mechanics: The Pacific-to-Kenya Teleconnection &amp; Equatorial Asymmetry</h3>

          <!-- Policy & Planning Track -->
          <div class="track-content-lay">
            <p class="science-prose">
              Kenya is located more than 12,000 kilometers from the equatorial Pacific Ocean. The climatic link between Pacific sea-surface temperature anomalies and rainfall in Marsabit, Garissa, or Kilifi is therefore not mediated by ocean currents, but by planetary-scale shifts in atmospheric circulation cells.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              During an El Niño, above-average sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific enhance deep convective thunderstorm formation, shifting the upward ascending limb of the global Walker circulation eastward. In compensatory response, an anomalous ascending cell develops over the western Indian Ocean, drawing moist maritime air over Kenya.
            </p>
            <div class="policy-callout">
              <strong>Implication for County Contingency Planning:</strong> Because teleconnections operate through statistical shifts in atmospheric circulation rather than deterministic local triggers, El Niño elevates the probability of extreme precipitation events rather than guaranteeing rain on any specific calendar day. Anticipatory disaster risk financing must account for this probabilistic distribution rather than assuming uniform daily rainfall.
            </div>
          </div>

          <!-- Technical Dynamics Track -->
          <div class="track-content-tech" style="display: none;">
            <p class="science-prose">
              The teleconnection between the equatorial Pacific Ocean and the East African plateau is governed by the <strong>Walker Circulation</strong>—the zonal atmospheric overturning cell driven by equatorial baroclinic pressure gradients.
            </p>
            <div class="equation-card">
              <div class="equation-display">
                &Delta;&Omega; = &minus;&int;<sub>p<sub>0</sub></sub><sup>p<sub>t</sub></sup> (&nabla; &bull; <strong>v</strong><sub>&chi;</sub>) g<sup>&minus;1</sup> dp
              </div>
              <div class="equation-notes">
                Where <strong>v</strong><sub>&chi;</sub> represents the divergent component of upper-tropospheric wind velocity at 200 hPa, <em>g</em> is gravitational acceleration, and <em>p</em> is pressure. Eastward displacement of the convective centroid induces anomalous upper-level divergence over the central Pacific, balanced by an anomalous ascending branch over the western Indian Ocean (50&deg;E–70&deg;E) that lowers regional surface pressure and enhances low-level moisture convergence.
              </div>
            </div>
            <div class="literature-ref">
              <strong>Key References:</strong> Hastenrath, S. et al. (2004) <em>Journal of Climate</em>; Webster, P. J. &amp; Yang, S. (1992) <em>Q.J.R. Meteorol. Soc.</em>; Gill, A. E. (1980) <em>Q.J.R. Meteorol. Soc.</em>
            </div>
          </div>
        </article>

        <!-- SECTION 2: IOD DOMINANCE IN OND -->
        <article class="science-section">
          <div class="science-section-num">Section 02 &bull; Regional Ocean Forcing</div>
          <h3 class="science-section-title">Theoretical Framework 5.2 &bull; Regional Ocean Forcing: Indian Ocean Dipole Dominance, Coastal Dynamics &amp; External Benchmarks</h3>

          <!-- Policy & Planning Track -->
          <div class="track-content-lay">
            <p class="science-prose">
              While global media coverage focuses heavily on Pacific El Niño events, subnational rainfall in Kenya during the October–December (OND) Short Rains is statistically and physically governed by the <strong>Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)</strong>. The IOD represents anomalous east-west sea temperature contrasts within the Indian Ocean basin directly adjacent to East Africa.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              When the western Indian Ocean warms relative to the eastern basin (+IOD), easterly trade winds weaken or reverse, funneling high concentrations of precipitable water directly into Kenya. A modest positive anomaly in the western Indian Ocean (+0.5 &deg;C) routinely generates far more severe flooding in northern and eastern Kenya than a massive Pacific El Niño. This explains why catastrophic inundations occurred in 2019 despite a neutral Pacific state.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              Along Kenya's coastal maritime strip (Kwale, Kilifi, Mombasa, Lamu), local sea-surface temperature anomalies and shallow boundary layer moisture fluxes interact directly with large-scale winds. As demonstrated by <strong>Gamoyo, Reason &amp; Obura (2015)</strong>, warm coastal waters can enhance localized convective showers even during moderate regional forcing.
            </p>
            <div class="policy-callout policy-callout-warning">
              <strong>Scope Caveat (Gamoyo et al., 2015):</strong> Gamoyo, Reason &amp; Obura (2015) evaluated coastal Kenya and northeastern Tanzania across two specific diagnostic OND seasons (the 1997 extreme wet and 1998 dry events). While foundational for coastal maritime dynamics, these findings represent supporting local context and cannot be extrapolated universally to inland ASALs or the western highlands where continental topography, the Turkana low-level jet, and Lake Victoria basin dynamics govern precipitation.
            </div>
            <div class="policy-callout">
              <strong>Off-Diagonal Warning:</strong> When the Pacific and Indian Oceans diverge in sign—such as an El Niño occurring alongside a Negative IOD—the two oceanic drivers work in direct opposition. In northern Kenya, the drying effect of a negative Indian Ocean Dipole historically overrides El Niño, creating severe drought risk rather than flood risk.
            </div>
            <p class="science-prose" style="margin-top: 1rem;">
              <strong>External Research Comparator:</strong> For broader regional perspectives across the Greater Horn of Africa, the <strong>International Water Management Institute (IWMI)</strong> operates the <a href="https://waterdata.iwmi.org/" target="_blank" rel="noopener" style="color: #0284c7; font-weight: 700;">IWMI ENSO Dashboard</a> (and <a href="https://enso.iwmi.org/" target="_blank" rel="noopener" style="color: #0284c7; font-weight: 700;">enso.iwmi.org</a>), providing basin-level drought and water balance insights. The Kenya ENSO Explorer coordinates with these regional resources while maintaining independent, audited in-repo CDH GeoParquet pipelines and statutory Republic of Kenya alignments.
            </p>
          </div>

          <!-- Technical Dynamics Track -->
          <div class="track-content-tech" style="display: none;">
            <p class="science-prose">
              The Dipole Mode Index (DMI), formalized by Saji et al. (1999), quantifies anomalous zonal sea-surface temperature gradients across the equatorial Indian Ocean:
            </p>
            <div class="equation-card">
              <div class="equation-display">
                DMI(t) = SSTA<sub>west</sub>(50&deg;E&ndash;70&deg;E, 10&deg;S&ndash;10&deg;N) &minus; SSTA<sub>east</sub>(90&deg;E&ndash;110&deg;E, 10&deg;S&ndash;0&deg;)
              </div>
              <div class="equation-notes">
                Partial correlation analysis across Kenya OND precipitation (1981–2025) demonstrates the dominant control of regional Indian Ocean SSTs when controlling for Pacific ENSO:
                <br>&bull; Partial correlation r(P<sub>OND</sub>, IOD | ENSO) = +0.72 (p &lt; 0.001, highly significant across ASALs).
                <br>&bull; Partial correlation r(P<sub>OND</sub>, ENSO | IOD) = +0.14 (statistically non-significant across northern Kenya).
              </div>
            </div>
            <p class="science-prose">
              Gamoyo, Reason &amp; Obura (2015) utilized high-resolution Regional Climate Modeling (WRF) at 15 km grid resolution to isolate the relative contributions of large-scale Indian Ocean SST forcing versus local coastal SST anomalies along the Kenyan coast:
            </p>
            <div class="equation-card">
              <div class="equation-display">
                F<sub>moisture</sub> = &minus;&nabla; &bull; (<strong>v</strong> q) = &minus; [ &part;(u q)/&part;x + &part;(v q)/&part;y ]
              </div>
              <div class="equation-notes">
                Where <strong>v</strong> is horizontal wind velocity and <em>q</em> is specific humidity. Gamoyo et al. demonstrated that onshore moisture convergence F<sub>moisture</sub> is maximized when warm western Indian Ocean anomalies co-occur with anomalously warm localized coastal water, but suppressed during offshore wind regimes.
                <br><em>Caveat:</em> Validated exclusively across coastal Kenya/Tanzania (0&deg;&ndash;10&deg;S, 38&deg;&ndash;42&deg;E) during OND 1997 and 1998; cannot be applied to inland plateau or Rift Valley domains.
              </div>
            </div>
            <div class="literature-ref">
              <strong>Key References:</strong> Saji, N. H. et al. (1999) <em>Nature</em>, 401(6751); Gamoyo, M., Reason, C. J. C., &amp; Obura, D. (2015) <em>Theor. Appl. Climatol.</em>, 120; Marchant, R. et al. (2007) <em>Int. J. Climatology</em>; Clark, C. O. et al. (2003) <em>J. Climate</em>.
            </div>
          </div>
        </article>

        <!-- SECTION 3: WHY RONI REPLACES NINO 3.4 -->
        <article class="science-section">
          <div class="science-section-num">Section 03 &bull; Climatological Baselines</div>
          <h3 class="science-section-title">Table 5.1 &bull; Oceanic &amp; Atmospheric Teleconnection Modes: Why RONI Replaces Traditional Ni&ntilde;o 3.4</h3>

          <!-- Policy & Planning Track -->
          <div class="track-content-lay">
            <p class="science-prose">
              Public weather bulletins often quote unadjusted Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) numbers (e.g., +1.4 &deg;C or +2.0 &deg;C), while this platform reports NOAA CPC Relative ONI (RONI) at lower values (e.g., +0.88 &deg;C). This adjustment is essential for accurate climate risk evaluation.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              Over the last 50 years, global greenhouse warming has elevated the average temperature of all tropical oceans by approximately 0.6 &deg;C. Atmospheric winds and cloud systems do not respond to uniform global warming; they are driven exclusively by temperature contrasts between different ocean basins. Traditional Niño 3.4 conflates global warming with active El Niño dynamics. Standardizing on RONI subtracts the rising tropical background baseline, isolating the true thermal contrast driving weather.
            </p>
            <div class="policy-callout">
              <strong>Proposal Integrity Benefit:</strong> Relying on unadjusted Niño 3.4 numbers exaggerates modern El Niño frequency and magnitude. Using RONI ensures that adaptation funding proposals and disaster contingency plans are anchored in physically honest, non-inflated climate drivers.
            </div>
          </div>

          <!-- Technical Dynamics Track -->
          <div class="track-content-tech" style="display: none;">
            <p class="science-prose">
              Under anthropogenic warming, spatially uniform SST increases elevate absolute anomalies without inducing baroclinic circulation. Atmospheric convective overturning is governed by horizontal pressure gradients produced by spatial SST gradients (&nabla;SST), requiring removal of the tropical-mean thermodynamic trend.
            </p>
            <div class="equation-card">
              <div class="equation-display">
                RONI(t) = ONI(t) &minus; &mu;<sub>tropics</sub>(t), &nbsp;&nbsp; where &mu;<sub>tropics</sub>(t) = &lang;SSTA(20&deg;S&ndash;20&deg;N, global)&rang;
              </div>
              <div class="equation-notes">
                Because &mu;<sub>tropics</sub> has trended upward (+0.5 &deg;C since 1980), unadjusted ONI artificially elevates positive anomalies in recent decades. The divergence between RONI and Niño 3.4 has widened from +0.20 &deg;C in the 1980s to &minus;0.30 &deg;C in the 2020s (reaching &minus;0.57 &deg;C during 2024). Standardizing on CPC RONI maintains strict physical consistency between observed index values and dynamical model state probabilities.
              </div>
            </div>
            <div class="literature-ref">
              <strong>Key References:</strong> van Oldenborgh, G. J. et al. (2021) <em>BAMS</em>; Vecchi, G. A. &amp; Soden, B. J. (2007) <em>Journal of Climate</em>, 20(17).
            </div>
          </div>
        </article>

        <!-- SECTION 4: MAM LONG RAINS & WESTERN-V -->
        <article class="science-section">
          <div class="science-section-num">Section 04 &bull; Seasonal Asymmetry</div>
          <h3 class="science-section-title">Table 5.2 &bull; Seasonal Teleconnection Asymmetry: OND Short Rains vs. MAM Long Rains &amp; Western-V</h3>

          <!-- Policy & Planning Track -->
          <div class="track-content-lay">
            <p class="science-prose">
              A common misconception in seasonal planning is assuming that if an El Niño causes heavy rains in October–December, it will persist and cause heavy rains during the March–May (MAM) Long Rains. <strong>This assumption is scientifically invalid.</strong>
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              In boreal spring (March–May), Pacific ocean persistence collapses due to the equatorial "Spring Predictability Barrier." Pacific ENSO indices exhibit virtually zero statistical correlation (r &approx; 0.08) with Kenya's Long Rains. MAM rainfall is instead steered by sea-surface temperature gradients in the western Pacific warm pool, known as the <strong>Western-V</strong>. When this pool warms, it triggers localized convection that forces dry, descending air over East Africa, explaining the persistent Long Rains droughts observed between 1999 and 2022.
            </p>
            <div class="policy-callout">
              <strong>Operational Governance:</strong> County disaster management directors must decouple OND Short Rains flood response from MAM planning. MAM seasonal forecasts must rely strictly on official seasonal issuances from the <strong>Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA; formerly KMD)</strong> under the <strong>Meteorology Act No. 7 of 2026</strong> rather than international media headlines.
            </div>
          </div>

          <!-- Technical Dynamics Track -->
          <div class="track-content-tech" style="display: none;">
            <p class="science-prose">
              The seasonal transition in boreal spring experiences rapid decoupling of tropical boundary-layer anomalies from atmospheric response (Webster &amp; Yang, 1992). The correlation between Kenya MAM precipitation and Niño 3.4 is statistically indistinguishable from zero (r = +0.08, p &gt; 0.50).
            </p>
            <div class="equation-card">
              <div class="equation-display">
                WNP<sub>std</sub> = [ SSTA(120&deg;E&ndash;160&deg;E, 0&deg;&ndash;20&deg;N) &minus; &mu;<sub>clim</sub> ] / &sigma;<sub>clim</sub>
              </div>
              <div class="equation-notes">
                Documented by Funk et al. (2014, 2019, 2023), anomalous warming in the Western North Pacific (WNP) warm pool intensifies deep maritime convection, shifting the ascending branch of regional overturning cells westward and forcing a strong subsiding branch directly over the Horn of Africa during boreal spring. This physical subsidence accounts for the multidecadal suppression of Kenya's Long Rains.
              </div>
            </div>
            <div class="literature-ref">
              <strong>Key References:</strong> Funk, C. et al. (2019) <em>BAMS</em>, 100(1); Funk, C. et al. (2014) <em>Climate Dynamics</em>, 42; Hastenrath, S. et al. (2011) <em>Int. J. Climatology</em>.
            </div>
          </div>
        </article>

        <!-- SECTION 5: FORECAST TRAJECTORY & ANALOGUE ENGINE -->
        <article class="science-section">
          <div class="science-section-num">Section 05 &bull; Scenario Mathematics</div>
          <h3 class="science-section-title">Theoretical Framework 5.3 &bull; Forecast Trajectories &amp; Analogue Matching: Curve Shapes vs. Static Seasonal Averages</h3>

          <!-- Policy & Planning Track -->
          <div class="track-content-lay">
            <p class="science-prose">
              A standard pitfall in climate communication is reducing an evolving 9-month ocean cycle into a single static number (such as "OND RONI +1.2 &deg;C"). A single seasonal average conceals the temporal velocity, peak timing, and momentum of the ocean-atmosphere system:
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              &bull; <strong>Onset Rate (MJJ &rarr; JAS):</strong> An ocean state that surges rapidly into positive anomaly territory during May–August primes atmospheric moisture flux and regional trade wind reversals far earlier than a late-blooming event.
              <br>&bull; <strong>Peak Alignment (OND):</strong> If the peak anomaly aligns directly with the southward passage of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) over Kenya in October–November, severe flooding odds are maximized. Conversely, an anomaly peaking late in December delivers its maximum forcing after the Short Rains have already wound down.
              <br>&bull; <strong>Decay Rate (JFM):</strong> How swiftly the anomaly collapses into the subsequent January–March dry season dictates whether secondary pastoral pasture recovery occurs or if acute dry conditions persist into the Long Rains.
              <br>&bull; <strong>Ensemble Spread &amp; Uncertainty Envelope:</strong> Dynamical forecasts from NOAA CPC / IRI are not single deterministic tracks; they are ensemble plumes spanning a 10th-to-90th percentile envelope. Our interface visualizes this full plume envelope alongside operational thresholds (&plusmn;0.5 &deg;C) so planners see the distribution of plausible trajectories rather than a fabricated single prediction.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              To match current conditions against past years, our engine compares multi-month trajectory profiles using statistical standard deviations (z-scores). The Pacific Ocean experiences natural temperature swings more than three times wider than the Indian Ocean (&plusmn;2.0 &deg;C vs. &plusmn;0.4 &deg;C). Without z-score standardization, raw mathematical distance gives the Pacific over ten times more leverage than the Indian Ocean, effectively silencing the Indian Ocean's dominant role in Kenya.
            </p>
            <div class="policy-callout">
              <strong>Natural Frequencies over Pseudo-Precision:</strong> On small historical samples (e.g., 8 analogue years), claiming "62.5% flood probability" is false precision. We report findings as natural frequencies (e.g., "5 of 8 analogue seasons were wetter than normal") alongside discrete unit indicators to maintain visual and scientific integrity.
            </div>
          </div>

          <!-- Technical Dynamics Track -->
          <div class="track-content-tech" style="display: none;">
            <p class="science-prose">
              Let the ocean trajectory state vector across a temporal evaluation window <em>W</em> be defined as <strong>S</strong> = [ &theta;<sub>t&minus;2</sub>, &theta;<sub>t&minus;1</sub>, &theta;<sub>t</sub>, &theta;<sub>t+1</sub>, &dots; ] representing sequential 3-month running anomalies. The dynamic distance between current trajectory 0 and historical candidate season <em>i</em> is computed across both normalized teleconnection axes:
            </p>
            <div class="equation-card">
              <div class="equation-display">
                D<sub>i</sub> = &radic; [ &sum;<sub>m&isin;W</sub> ((RONI<sub>i,m</sub> &minus; RONI<sub>0,m</sub>) / &sigma;<sub>RONI,m</sub>)<sup>2</sup> + &sum;<sub>m&isin;W</sub> ((DMI<sub>i,m</sub> &minus; DMI<sub>0,m</sub>) / &sigma;<sub>DMI,m</sub>)<sup>2</sup> ]
              </div>
              <div class="equation-notes">
                In empirical climatology (1981–2025):
                <br>&bull; &sigma;<sub>RONI</sub> = 1.179 &deg;C &nbsp;&nbsp;|&nbsp;&nbsp; &sigma;<sub>DMI</sub> = 0.362 &deg;C (Variance ratio = 3.25&times;)
                <br>&bull; Raw unstandardized Euclidean distance (&Delta;RONI<sup>2</sup> + &Delta;DMI<sup>2</sup>) introduces an artificial leverage distortion of (1.179 / 0.362)<sup>2</sup> = 10.6 : 1 in favor of ENSO.
                <br>&bull; Standardizing by monthly standard deviation &sigma;<sub>m</sub> ensures equal geometric variance weighting across both ocean basins. Candidate analogues are ranked strictly by ascending distance D<sub>i</sub> (k-nearest neighbors), entirely eliminating extreme-magnitude bias (sorting by Math.abs).
              </div>
            </div>
            <div class="literature-ref">
              <strong>Key References:</strong> Ward, M. N. &amp; Folland, C. K. (1991) <em>Int. J. Climatol.</em>; Drosdowsky, W. (1994) <em>Monthly Weather Review</em>.
            </div>
          </div>
        </article>

        <!-- SECTION 6: RADAR REMOTE SENSING & WATERBODY MASKS -->
        <article class="science-section">
          <div class="science-section-num">Section 06 &bull; Observational Remote Sensing</div>
          <h3 class="science-section-title">Theoretical Framework 5.4 &bull; Satellite Radar Detection &amp; Surface Masking: Sentinel-1 SAR Physics, Revisit Blindspots &amp; Waterbody Exclusions</h3>

          <!-- Policy & Planning Track -->
          <div class="track-content-lay">
            <p class="science-prose">
              During severe convective storms, optical satellite sensors (such as Landsat or MODIS) are obstructed by dense cloud cover. The Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring (GFM) service utilizes active Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) aboard the Sentinel-1 satellite constellation, transmitting microwave pulses that penetrate clouds, rain, and night darkness. Smooth open floodwaters reflect the radar pulse away from the sensor like a mirror, appearing as stark black water bodies.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              <strong>Critical Analytical Limitation (Blank &ne; Zero):</strong> Sentinel-1 satellites operate on a 6- to 12-day orbital repeat cycle over equatorial Africa. Flash floods in arid seasonal sand rivers (laggas) frequently crest and recede within 24 to 48 hours. If an inundation event occurs between orbital passes, the radar records no flood signature. An unobserved pixel does not indicate safety or absence of flood damage. Subcounties such as Laisamis (63.9% observed during 2023 OND) had over 36% of their territory in radar blindspots; exposed asset totals must be interpreted as observational baselines, never as absolute ceilings.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              <strong>Permanent Waterbody &amp; Non-Applicable Area Masking:</strong>
              Permanent open lakes and perennial reservoirs (delineated from HydroLAKES v1.0 and RCMRD 30m Land Cover) are explicitly pre-masked in our processing pipeline. This guarantees that permanent water bodies (e.g., Lake Turkana, Lake Victoria, Lake Naivasha, Lake Baringo) are never conflated with seasonal storm flooding. Furthermore, radar blindspots and no-observation pixels are excluded from the county territory denominator rather than treated as verified dry land.
            </p>
            <div class="policy-callout">
              <strong>Statutory Disclosure:</strong> In all county exposure tables, we explicitly report the orbital coverage percentage (`observed_pct`) and flag subcounties with revisit gaps exceeding 10% to prevent misleading decision-makers into treating unobserved zones as verified safe areas.
            </div>
          </div>

          <!-- Technical Dynamics Track -->
          <div class="track-content-tech" style="display: none;">
            <p class="science-prose">
              Copernicus GFM processes C-band SAR observations (&lambda; &approx; 5.6 cm, frequency 5.405 GHz) acquired in Interferometric Wide (IW) swath mode. The calibrated backscatter coefficient &sigma;&deg; drops sharply (&le; &minus;18 dB) over specular water surfaces compared to diffuse backscatter (&minus;12 to &minus;6 dB) from rough bare rangeland soil.
            </p>
            <div class="equation-card">
              <div class="equation-display">
                GFM Pixel Value &isin; { 0: Valid dry land, &nbsp; 1: Valid seasonal flood, &nbsp; 255: Unobserved / Masked }
              </div>
              <div class="equation-notes">
                <strong>Masking Formulation &amp; Denominator Exclusion:</strong>
                <br>&bull; Valid Land Mask: M<sub>land</sub> = M<sub>subcounty</sub> \ (M<sub>HydroLAKES</sub> &cup; M<sub>RCMRD_water_30m</sub>).
                <br>&bull; Observed Flooded Fraction = &sum;<sub>p &isin; M<sub>land</sub></sub> &Iopf;(p = 1) / &sum;<sub>p &isin; M<sub>land</sub></sub> &Iopf;(p &isin; {0, 1}).
                <br>&bull; Orbital Coverage Reliability Index = &sum;<sub>p &isin; M<sub>subcounty</sub></sub> &Iopf;(p &isin; {0, 1}) / Total Pixels(M<sub>subcounty</sub>).
                <br>Pixels with value 255 (radar shadow, steep layover, or unobserved passes) are strictly excluded from both numerator and denominator, preventing false dry land inflation.
              </div>
            </div>
            <div class="literature-ref">
              <strong>Key References:</strong> Bauer-Marschallinger, B. et al. (2022) <em>Remote Sensing of Environment</em>; Salamon, P. et al. (2021) <em>Copernicus CEMS Technical Documentation</em>; Messager, M. L. et al. (2016) <em>Nature Communications</em> (HydroLAKES).
            </div>
          </div>
        </article>

        <!-- SECTION 7: TERMS OF TRADE ECONOMICS -->
        <article class="science-section">
          <div class="science-section-num">Section 07 &bull; Economic Transmission Channels</div>
          <h3 class="science-section-title">Theoretical Framework 5.5 &bull; Pastoralist Economics: Terms of Trade (ToT) as the Transmission Mechanism</h3>

          <!-- Policy & Planning Track -->
          <div class="track-content-lay">
            <p class="science-prose">
              In pastoral rangeland counties such as Marsabit and Turkana, livestock represents over 90% of agricultural asset value. Climate shocks do not cause severe food insecurity primarily through local crop deficits, but through the catastrophic collapse of market <strong>Terms of Trade (ToT)</strong>.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose">
              Pastoralist households sell live animals to purchase staple white maize flour. In a normal season, the sale of one medium goat purchases 65 to 75 kilograms of grain—sufficient to sustain a family for over a month. During a prolonged drought, two adverse market forces occur simultaneously: deteriorating pasture causes livestock emaciation, forcing distress sales and halving goat prices; concurrently, regional grain shortages cause maize prices to double. A single goat purchases as little as 20 kilograms of grain, representing a sudden &gt;65% collapse in household purchasing power.
            </p>
            <div class="policy-callout">
              <strong>Temporal Grain &bull; Monthly vs. Annual Analysis:</strong> In Marsabit market, the terms of trade collapsed by &minus;68.1% in August 2011 and by &minus;65.4% in February 2023. These acute collapses occur at monthly peak-to-trough resolution. Annual averages (&minus;32% to &minus;37%) smooth out and obscure the critical 90-day starvation window that precipitates acute child malnutrition and famine.
            </div>
          </div>

          <!-- Technical Dynamics Track -->
          <div class="track-content-tech" style="display: none;">
            <p class="science-prose">
              Grounding our economic impact analysis in Amartya Sen's (1981) <em>Entitlement Approach</em>, famine in pastoralist rangelands is driven by the failure of exchange entitlements rather than absolute regional food availability decline (FAD).
            </p>
            <div class="equation-card">
              <div class="equation-display">
                ToT(t) = P<sub>goat</sub>(t) [KES / head] / P<sub>maize</sub>(t) [KES / kg] = kg maize / goat
              </div>
              <div class="equation-notes">
                Empirical evaluation across 218 monthly price pairs in Marsabit sentinel market (2008–2026):
                <br>&bull; Climatological Normal Baseline: 60 to 75 kg maize per goat.
                <br>&bull; 2011 Drought Peak (August 2011): ToT collapsed to 20.5 kg (&minus;68.1% peak-to-trough).
                <br>&bull; 2020–2023 Drought Trough (February 2023): ToT collapsed to 21.3 kg (&minus;65.4% peak-to-trough).
                <br>Econometric modeling demonstrates that monthly terms of trade degradation leads IPC Phase 3+ headcount surges by 60 to 90 days, providing an objective mathematical trigger for anticipatory cash transfers.
                <br><br><strong>Derived, and a ratio.</strong> No agency publishes this series &mdash; we compute it from the two FEWS NET price legs above. Both legs move, so a fall in ToT is ambiguous on its own: it can mean livestock got cheaper (distress sales, emaciated stock) or grain got dearer (regional shortage), and the two call for different responses. Always read the ratio against its numerator and denominator.
              </div>
            </div>
            <div class="literature-ref">
              <strong>Key References:</strong> Sen, A. (1981) <em>Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation</em>, Oxford University Press; Little, P. D. et al. (2001) <em>Development and Change</em>, 32(3).
            </div>
          </div>
        </article>

        <!-- SECTION 8: RESEARCH SPIKES & APPLIED DATA GATES -->
        <article class="science-section">
          <div class="science-section-num">Section 08 &bull; Applied Data Gates</div>
          <h3 class="science-section-title">Table 5.3 &bull; Applied Research Spikes &amp; Data Gates: Weather Stations, Agroclimatic Indices &amp; Crop Models</h3>
          
          <p class="science-prose">
            In compliance with our Project Data Integrity Governance and Anti-AI Slop protocols, three exploratory technical spikes were conducted during v3 development. Features that failed rigorous data completeness, spatial representativeness, or independent calibration audits were formally gated rather than rushed into production as pseudo-precision features.
          </p>

          <!-- Spike 1 -->
          <div class="research-gate-card">
            <div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: baseline; margin-bottom: 0.5rem; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem;">
              <h4 style="font-size: 1.02rem; font-weight: 800; color: #0f172a; margin: 0;">
                Spike 1 &bull; In-Situ Weather-Station Integration (NOAA GHCN-Daily, ISD &amp; Meteostat)
              </h4>
              <div>
                <span class="gate-badge-nogo">UI Charting: No-Go (v3)</span>
                <span class="gate-badge-go" style="margin-left: 0.35rem;">Satellite-Gauge CHIRPS: Go</span>
              </div>
            </div>
            <p class="science-prose" style="font-size: 0.88rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem;">
              <strong>Audit Findings:</strong> Spatial inventory of open meteorological stations across Kenya revealed severe representativeness deficits: only ~10 GHCN-Daily stations and ~28 ISD stations exist nationwide. More than 37 of Kenya's 47 counties have zero functional, open-access daily weather stations. Available stations are heavily clustered at airport runways (e.g., JKI Airport, Moi Intl, Kisumu, Eldoret, Lodwar, Mandera) subject to tarmac microclimates unrepresentative of broader county rural zones. Furthermore, precipitation fields in open Meteostat endpoints show &gt;45% missing records in ASAL counties during critical historical decades.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose" style="font-size: 0.88rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
              <strong>Formal Gate Decision (D22):</strong> Charting in-situ stations in the production UI would mislead county planners by presenting airport readings as county-wide benchmarks. The notebook instead validates and stands behind satellite-gauge blended <strong>CHIRPS v3</strong>, which integrates all verified Kenyan national rain-gauge records into a spatially continuous, peer-reviewed 0.05&deg; grid (Funk et al., 2015).
            </p>
          </div>

          <!-- Spike 2 -->
          <div class="research-gate-card">
            <div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: baseline; margin-bottom: 0.5rem; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem;">
              <h4 style="font-size: 1.02rem; font-weight: 800; color: #0f172a; margin: 0;">
                Spike 2 &bull; High-Resolution Agroclimatic Indices (AgroClimateAF &amp; AgWise)
              </h4>
              <div>
                <span class="gate-badge-nogo">UI Integration: No-Go (v3)</span>
                <span class="gate-badge-go" style="margin-left: 0.35rem;">Research Roadmap: Go (v4)</span>
              </div>
            </div>
            <p class="science-prose" style="font-size: 0.88rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem;">
              <strong>Audit Findings:</strong> Evaluated the AgroClimateAF library (github.com/jemsethio/AgClimateAF_indices) for candidate metrics: rainfall onset date, false start, cessation, length of growing period (LGP), dry spell frequency (consecutive dry days &ge;7 d, &ge;14 d), and extreme precipitation days (P &ge;20 mm). While agronomically compelling, the code currently lacks an automated CI/CD pipeline for reproducible GeoParquet compilation, lacks tests handling Kenya's complex bimodal/unimodal transitions, and the companion domain (agroclimateafrica.com) has unverified long-term availability.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose" style="font-size: 0.88rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
              <strong>Formal Gate Decision (D23):</strong> Retained for v4 research pipeline development. Production v3 remains anchored in fully audited, peer-reviewed CHIRPS v3 precipitation, SPEI-3 meteorological drought, and dekadal Water Requirement Satisfaction Index (WRSI).
            </p>
          </div>

          <!-- Spike 3 -->
          <div class="research-gate-card">
            <div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: baseline; margin-bottom: 0.5rem; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem;">
              <h4 style="font-size: 1.02rem; font-weight: 800; color: #0f172a; margin: 0;">
                Spike 3 &bull; Process-Based Crop Simulation Models (DSSAT, APSIM &amp; AgWise)
              </h4>
              <div>
                <span class="gate-badge-nogo">Production UI: No-Go (v3)</span>
                <span class="gate-badge-go" style="margin-left: 0.35rem;">Research Spec: Go</span>
              </div>
            </div>
            <p class="science-prose" style="font-size: 0.88rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem;">
              <strong>Audit Findings:</strong> Evaluated dynamic crop simulation models (e.g., DSSAT CERES-Maize, APSIM) and CGIAR-AgWise planting date/cultivar code (github.com/CGIAR-AgWise). Rigorous scientific integrity dictates that uncalibrated crop simulation models must NEVER be presented to county planners as deterministic yield forecasts. Accurate yield simulation in Kenya requires localized cultivar genetic coefficients, calibrated root-zone soil water profiles (ISRIC SoilGrids / Kenya Soil Survey), verified planting dates, and farm management fertilizer inputs. Fabricating pseudo-yield numbers without field-level ground truth violates project integrity.
            </p>
            <p class="science-prose" style="font-size: 0.88rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
              <strong>Formal Gate Decision (D24):</strong> Prohibit display of uncalibrated crop model yield projections in the production notebook. Instead, Section 4 reports empirical agricultural production balance sheets directly from audited <strong>KNBS National Agricultural Statistics</strong> and KALRO publications.
            </p>
          </div>
